paragraphs.text: John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople. From the exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew. On the next day, which was after Friday, the chief priests and Pharisees gathered before Pilate, saying: “We remember that while that deceiver was still alive, he said, ‘After three days I will rise.’ Therefore command that the tomb be secured until the third day, lest his disciples come by night and steal him and tell the people, ‘He has risen from the dead.’ Then the last deception will be worse than the first.” Deception blinds itself at every turn, and unwillingly helps the truth. Now consider: it was necessary to believe that he died, that he was buried, and that he rose. And all this comes about through his enemies. Look, then, at these words, which bear witness to all this: “We remember that that deceiver said, while still

alive.” So he is dead. “After three days I will rise. Command that the tomb be secured.” So he has also been buried. “Lest his disciples come and steal him.” Therefore, if the tomb is sealed, there will be no deception at all. Thus the proof of the resurrection is also beyond dispute—the matter about which you spoke at length. For since you sealed it, there could be no deception. And if there was no deception at all, then clearly and indisputably he has risen. See how, even unwillingly, they labor to establish the truth. Now consider how the disciples love the truth: they conceal nothing of what their enemies say, even when they say insulting things. For here they even call him a deceiver, and the disciples do not keep this from you. This reveals both the foolishness of those men and the innocent, truth-loving character of the disciples. For even his death did not put an end to their anger. It is also worth examining this: where did he say, “After three days I will rise”? For no one will find it stated so plainly. But there is the parable of Jonah. Thus they understood what was being said, and they did evil deliberately. What, then, did Pilate say? “Do you have a guard? Secure it as best you know how.” And they secured it, sealing the tomb along with the guards. He did not let the soldiers alone seal it. Having learned about him, he did not want to be involved with them, but wanted to be rid of them. That is why he did this and said, “Seal it yourselves however you wish, so that you may not have others to

blame.” For if the soldiers alone had sealed it, They could have said this, even though their words were false and unconvincing. Nevertheless, just as they felt no shame in other matters, they would have spoken this way about this too: that the soldiers, by allowing the body to be stolen, had enabled the disciples to invent a story about the resurrection. But now, having made it secure themselves, they cannot even say that. Do you see how much they advance the truth, even against their will? For it was they who came, they who made the request, and they who sealed it and posted a guard, so that each became an accuser and a witness against the other. [?] And when could they have stolen it—on the Sabbath? And how? For it was not lawful to approach. Even if they had broken the law, how would men who were so frightened have dared to approach? And how could they have persuaded anyone? By saying what? By doing what? With what encouragement would they have been willing to stand up for a dead man? What reward did they expect from him? What recompense? While he was still alive, they fled when they saw him bound. And after his death would they have been willing to act boldly on his behalf? If he had not risen, how could we understand their willingness to tell such a lie about a resurrection that had not happened? That is, because he had spoken to them at length about the resurrection, and had often said—as these men themselves also reported— “After three days I will rise.” So if he had not risen, it is clear that these men, having been deceived

and having fought against an entire nation on his behalf and become homeless and without a city, would have disowned him and would not have wished to bestow such glory on him, having been deceived and having fallen into the gravest troubles, having fallen into troubles because of him. And that they could not have fabricated this if there had been no resurrection needs no argument. For what were they relying on? Skill with words? But they were less educated than anyone. Or wealth? But they had neither a staff nor sandals. Or noble birth? But they were poor men born to poor parents. Or a distinguished homeland? But they came from obscure places. Or their numbers? But there were no more than eleven of them, and even they were scattered. Or certain promises made by their teacher? For if he had not risen, those promises would not have seemed trustworthy to them either. And how could they have withstood a raging crowd? For their leader could not endure even a word from a woman who kept the gate. And all the others scattered as soon as they saw him bound. How, then, could they have planned to run to the ends of the world and establish a fabricated story about the resurrection? For if one could not endure a woman's threat, and another could not endure imprisonment, how could they stand against emperors, rulers, and crowds, against swords and gridirons, and furnaces, and countless deaths every day, unless they had

received their fill of [?] from the one who rose? There were so many signs and so many miracles, yet none of them put the Jews to shame. Instead, they crucified the one who performed them. Would they then have been willing to believe those who merely spoke about the resurrection? It is not so, certainly not. Rather, the power of the risen one accomplished this. Now consider their shameful wickedness. “We remembered,” they said, “that this deceiver said while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise.’” But if he was a deceiver and led people astray with lies, why are you afraid and running about, and why are you making such haste? “We are afraid,” they said, “that his disciples might steal him and deceive many people.” This too proved to have no reasonable basis at all. Nevertheless, wickedness is contentious and shameless, and undertakes senseless things. They ordered the tomb to be secured until the third day, as though contending over fixed terms and wanting to show that he had been a deceiver even before this. They extend their malice even to the grave. That is why he rose earlier, so that they could not say, “He lied and was stolen.” For there is no fault in rising earlier, whereas rising later would have been full of grounds for reproach. For if he had not risen then, while they were sitting there and keeping watch, but after they had gone away after three days, they would have had something to answer and say, however unreasonable. That is why he acted beforehand. For it was fitting that the resurrection should take place while they were sitting there and keeping watch, so that it

should indeed take place within the three days. But if it happened after the days had passed and the guards had gone away, the event would have been open to reproach. That is why he also permitted the seals, just as they wished. And soldiers sat on guard, and they did not care that they were doing this and working on the Sabbath. Instead, they looked to one thing alone: their own cunning, so that through it they might prevail. This is a sign of utter madness and of fear that shakes one completely. For the Jews who had seized him were afraid of him when he was dead. Yet if he were an ordinary man, they ought to have felt confident. But so that they might know that, while alive, he willingly suffered what he suffered, here are the seal, the stone, and the guard, and they could not hold him back. Only one thing comes of it: the tomb is exposed. and for the resurrection to be confirmed by this. For not only were the soldiers keeping watch; the Jews were also sitting nearby. Late on the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning, Mary Magdalene came, and the other Mary, to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, came forward, rolled the stone away from the entrance to the tomb, and sat on it. His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing was white as snow. The angel came after the resurrection. Why, then, did he come and roll away the stone? For the sake of the women, for they saw him at the tomb then. So that they might believe that he had risen, they then saw the tomb empty of his body. That is why he removed the stone. That is why

there was also an earthquake: so that they would wake up and stir. For they had come to pour oil on him, and this happened at night, so it was likely that some had fallen asleep. And why, for what reason, did he say, “Do not you be afraid”? First he drives away their fear, and then he speaks about the resurrection. The word “you” shows them great honor, and shows that terrible things await those who dared to do what they did, unless they repent. “For it is not you,” he said, “who should be afraid, but those who crucified him.” Having taken away their fear through both his words and his appearance—for he did not merely display a radiant appearance— he also brought this good news, saying, “I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified.” And he is not ashamed to call him crucified, for this is the beginning of good things. “He has risen.” How? “As he said.” “Even if you do not believe me, remember his words, so that you may not disbelieve me.” Then he gives another proof: “Come, see the place where he lay.” That is why he removed the stone, so that the two women might obtain evidence from this as well. “And tell the disciples that you will see him in Galilee.” He arranges for them to bring the good news to others too, which made the two women believe all the more. And rightly in Galilee, to remove troubles and dangers, so that fear would not trouble their faith. And the two women went out of the tomb with fear and joy. Why? For they saw something [?] and marvelous: the empty tomb, where they had previously seen him laid. That is why he also led them to see it, so that the two women might be witnesses to both the tomb and the resurrection. For they were not merely thinking that no one had taken him away.

with many soldiers sitting there—unless he raised himself. For this reason they both rejoice and marvel, and at so long a delay. They receive the reward of being the first to see and to announce the good news. Not only what was spoken, but also what was seen. For since they went out with fear and joy, Jesus met them, saying, “Rejoice!” And the two women took hold of his feet, having run to him with exceedingly great joy. By holding him they also received a sign and assurance of the resurrection, and they worshiped him. What, then, does he say? “Do not be afraid.” Again he drives away their fear, opening the way for faith. “But go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me.” Notice how he too brings the good news to the disciples through these women, as I have often said, bringing the sex that had been especially dishonored into honor, giving it good hopes, and healing its suffering. [?] Would any of you wish to be like this and take hold of Jesus’ feet? Even now, as many of you as wish can do so, taking hold not only of his feet and hands, but even of that pure head, by partaking of the awe-inspiring mysteries with a pure conscience. And not only here, but on that other day too you will see him with that indescribable glory, coming with a host of angels, if you are willing to show kindness to others. And you will hear not only these words, “Rejoice!” but also those words: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you before the foundation

of the world.” Be kind to others, then, so that you may hear this. And you women who wear gold, seeing how those women ran, at least now, at last, put aside this disease of longing for gold. For if you wish to emulate the women, exchange the adornment with which you are clothed, clothing yourselves in mercy. Tell me, what benefit is there in these precious stones and garments embroidered with gold? “The soul rejoices and is glad in these things,” you say. I was asking you about the gain, but you tell me of the harm. For nothing is worse than celebrating these things, rejoicing in them, and clinging to them. For this cruel slavery becomes more bitter when someone rejoices even while enslaved. For when, as is fitting, will such a person devote himself to spiritual work? And when will he laugh, as he ought, at worldly concerns? as he considers it worthy of joy. To bind oneself with gold—never! But I beg you, let us put that aside and acquire mercy, which leads into the kingdom of heaven. May all of us attain it by the grace and love for humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
